connector: Peter has just opened the casket, and the room is very still. What comes out of it is not what Annemarie expected. Watch how carefully Peter hands things out, and notice a packet that changes hands without a word of explanation. Then look at the Rosens, in borrowed clothes, about to leave almost everything behind.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, this is Grete. The casket is open, and the night is not over yet. Peter has things to hand out, and a long, dark walk lies ahead for the Rosens. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 11, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: what does it cost to do the brave thing, even when it works?
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move asks you to be a little choosy. Not everything is a symbol, and a reader who calls everything a symbol isn’t really reading. Ask one question about each object you notice: does anyone in the story care about it? If nobody does, it’s probably there to help you see the room.
transcripts.dol: The model is about Peter, and a promise he can’t quite make. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together, and each one has two words pressed into one. Find where the first thought ends. Then give the second thought a capital to stand on.
transcripts.guide1: Today the word work moves from noticing to using. You’ve found the patterns. Now you put them to work: choosing when to press two words together, and splitting long words in the right place. A writer chooses on purpose. That’s what you’re practicing here.
transcripts.morphology: Halfway through the woods now. The path is darker here, under the trees. Four more words with the go-roots. One of them is the opposite of coming closer, like the tide pulling back from the beach. As you work, listen to each ending before you choose.
transcripts.vocabulary: Match these four again, and this time, say each word out loud in a sentence about Chapter 11 before you tap. If you can use a word, you own it. If you can only recognize it, it still belongs to the book.
transcripts.grammar: Here you get to choose. Pressing two words together changes how a sentence sounds, like the difference between a person talking and a sign on a wall. Fill in each blank. Then, in the last line, listen for whose voice you hear: a person, or a notice pinned to a door.
transcripts.spelling: Clap each word before you type anything, and count the claps. Then check your split against your claps. If your split makes a beat you didn’t clap, something’s wrong. Your ears are the best spelling check you have.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about letting go. When the Jewish family upstairs from us left in October 1943, they left the dishes on the table. Mrs. Levin pressed a little brass key into my mother’s hand and said, keep it for us. Watch the Rosens in this chapter. Notice what they had to leave behind, and what they carry with them anyway.
transcripts.read: Read slowly when the casket is opened. Watch what Peter takes out, and what he gives to each person. Notice the tiny passenger who needs something to keep her warm. And notice a small packet that changes hands without anyone explaining it. Ask yourself why nobody asks.
transcripts.rwm: Read this sentence aloud and feel where it slows down. Right in the middle, a little mark tells you a list is coming. Then three places, one after another, like steps. Ask why Lowry stops at three. Would two be enough? Would four be too many?
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. The questions ask about the packet Peter hands over, what the candlesticks stood for, and what Annemarie asks Peter when he says goodbye. Then, in your essay, you’ll tie each body paragraph back to your big idea with one strong closing sentence.
transcripts.chapter: Be careful with the third question. Peter does say goodbye. But Annemarie answers him with a question, and his answer is only half an answer. Think about what nobody could promise anybody in October 1943. That’s where your thinking should start.
transcripts.workshop: Each body paragraph needs a knot at the end, or the thread slips out. Today you add one closing sentence to each paragraph, using a key word from your claim. It’s a small sentence, but it reminds your reader why the whole paragraph matters.

a.raw: ellen couldnt say goodbye without crying it wasnt easy
a.fixed: Ellen couldn’t say goodbye without crying. It wasn’t easy.
a.why: A capital E on Ellen, an apostrophe in couldn’t (could + not), a period after the first sentence, a capital I to start the second, and an apostrophe in wasn’t (was + not).

b.raw: peter couldnt stay long there wasnt time
b.why: A capital P on Peter, an apostrophe in couldn’t (could + not), a period after the first sentence, a capital T to start the second, and an apostrophe in wasn’t (was + not).

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why Peter doesn’t tell Mr. Rosen what is inside.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain what the Rosens still carry with them, even without the candlesticks.
scholar.journal-q3: … and explain why Peter can’t give her a real promise.

g4w18cf1.h1: Two words: is and not. Which letter drops out when they squeeze together?
g4w18cf1.why: isn’t: is + not. The apostrophe stands where the o used to be.

g4w18cf2.h1: have + not. Keep all of have, then drop one letter from not.
g4w18cf2.why: haven’t: have + not, with the apostrophe in place of the o.

g4w18cf3.h1: We + will. Two letters disappear from will. Which ones?
g4w18cf3.why: We’ll: we + will. The apostrophe takes the place of the w and the i.

g4w18cf4.h1: could + not. Which letter from not goes missing?
g4w18cf4.why: couldn’t: could + not, with the apostrophe where the o was.

s4w18cf1.h1: Clap candle. Which letter has to stay with the le at the end?
s4w18cf1.why: can·dle: the d travels with le, so the first beat is can.

s4w18cf2.h1: Clap table. Which letter has to stay with the le at the end?
s4w18cf2.why: ta·ble: the b travels with le, so the first beat is ta.

s4w18cf3.h1: Clap bundle. Which letter has to stay with the le at the end?
s4w18cf3.why: bun·dle: the d travels with le, so the first beat is bun.

s4w18cf4.h1: Clap gentle. Which letter has to stay with the le at the end?
s4w18cf4.why: gen·tle: the t travels with le, so the first beat is gen.

match.proceed: Proceed has a go-root inside it. Look for the meaning about moving forward.
match.concede: Concede is about giving way. Look for the meaning about giving in.
match.access: Access is about getting in. Look for the meaning about a way to reach or enter.
match.symbol: A symbol is a real thing that stands for something bigger. Look for the meaning about standing for an idea.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. All three roots mean go, so let the spelling decide: listen to how each word ends.

why.t: On the night of Chapters 9 to 12, no lights are allowed at Uncle Henrik’s farm. The way to the harbor, past the apple tree, through the woods and across the meadow, has to be found in the dark. ceed, cede and cess are three spellings of one old root that means to go, so each right word shows you the next stretch of the path. One stretch each lesson, until it reaches the boat.

miss.fill1: Not quite. Only three words in English end in ceed: proceed, exceed and succeed. Is this one of them?
miss.fill2: Not quite. Most words that end with a ‘seed’ sound spell it cede. Only three use ceed. Try again.
miss.fill3: Not quite. Say the word out loud. Does it end with a ‘seed’ sound, or a ‘sess’ sound?
miss.fill4: Not quite. Most words that end with a ‘seed’ sound spell it cede. Only three use ceed. Try again.

wordgame.winDay: The path is through the woods, and the open meadow is ahead. One more lesson to reach the sea.
wordgame.win: The path comes out of the woods, crosses the meadow and reaches the harbor, where Uncle Henrik’s boat is waiting in the dark. ceed, cede and cess = go.

notes.wgrd: Not every detail is a symbol. A detail starts to stand for something when the story gives it weight: someone loves it, hides it, or hates to leave it behind.
vocab: To give in; to admit defeat or yield.
A way to reach or enter something.
An object or image that stands for an idea.
notes.wordParts: ceed, cede and cess are three spellings of one root that means “to go” or “to yield”: proceed, concede, access, process.
notes.grammar: Contractions make writing sound like a person talking. In dialogue they usually sound right. In formal writing, writers often spell the words out: do not instead of don’t.
notes.spelling: A consonant plus le at the end of a word is its own last beat, and the word splits just before that consonant: lit·tle, sim·ple. The endings -tion and -ture stay together the same way: ac·tion, pic·ture.

case.title: Candlesticks for the Sabbath
case.alt: Two tall silver candlesticks with round, curving bases, standing side by side in a dark museum case.
label: Candlesticks like these are lit on Friday evening, at sundown, to welcome Shabbat, the Jewish Sabbath. Many families pass a pair down from mother to daughter, so the same candlesticks light the same blessing for years and years.
This pair was made in Poland in the early 1900s. In Chapter 11, Annemarie remembers Mrs. Rosen lighting the Sabbath candles. When the Rosens fled, their candlesticks were left behind in Copenhagen.

look.q: Why might a family care more about its candlesticks than about a sofa or a bed?
look.a: They hold the family’s faith and memories. A sofa can be replaced. Years of Friday evenings cannot.

look.q: What can a family take with it, even when it can carry almost nothing?
look.a: Its memories, its faith, its pride, and the way its people treat each other. Chapter 11 shows this in the way the Rosens hold themselves.

case.credit: Silver-plated Sabbath candlesticks, Poland, early 20th century, at Beit Hatefutsot (the Museum of the Jewish People), Tel Aviv. Photo: Sodabottle, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
case.sub: A real object from a Jewish home.
